name: Don Quixote
kicker: Delusional knight of La Mancha · Parody of chivalric romance novels
briefing: A middle-aged Spanish gentleman reads so many tales of knights that he loses his grip on reality, renames himself a knight-errant, and rides off on his broken-down horse Rocinante to revive chivalry. With his practical squire Sancho Panza at his side, he battles windmills he mistakes for giants and showers devotion on an imaginary noblewoman, Dulcinea. Miguel de Cervantes’s _Don Quixote_ pokes fun at old romance novels while becoming one of the most influential novels ever written.

sample.note: the 16 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: This novel pretends to be translated from the notebooks of a made-up Arab historian, Cide Hamete Benengeli [“SEE-day ah-MEH-tay beh-nen-HEH-lee”]. Its title character drinks the Balsam of Fierabras [“fee-AY-rah-brahs”], a magic potion that is supposed to heal wounds, and becomes violently sick instead.
tossups.r: That same character later loses a climactic joust to a rival disguised as the Knight of the White Moon, which forces him to give up his adventures and go home. For 10 points, name this Spanish novel about a knight who attacks windmills, written by Miguel de Cervantes.

tossups.p: Early in Part Two of this novel, the title character jousts a disguised neighbor posing as the Knight of Mirrors and actually wins that round. This character also destroys a traveling puppeteer’s marionette show, convinced that its wooden villains are real soldiers he must defeat.
tossups.r: In Part One, he mistakes an ordinary barber’s metal washbasin for the magical Helmet of Mambrino [“mam-BREE-noh”]. For 10 points, name this novel whose title knight rides the horse Rocinante with his squire Sancho Panza, tilting at windmills he believes are giants.

tossups.p: Because of his sad, gaunt face, this novel’s title character earns the nickname the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance. Earlier, he attacks a group of traveling cloth merchants from Toledo after they refuse to swear that his imaginary lady-love is the most beautiful woman alive.
tossups.r: That lady-love is a peasant girl he renames Dulcinea and worships from afar. For 10 points, name this Miguel de Cervantes novel about a Spanish knight-errant who fights windmills with his squire, Sancho Panza.

tossups.p: As a prank, a duke makes this novel’s squire governor of the make-believe island of Barataria [“bah-rah-TAH-ree-ah”], fulfilling the title character’s old promise of an island. That same squire’s donkey, Dapple, is stolen and later recovered.
tossups.r: The title character himself is eventually beaten in a duel by the Knight of the White Moon and forced to return home. For 10 points, name this novel in which a delusional Spanish gentleman rides the horse Rocinante and attacks windmills, believing them to be giants.

tossups.p: In one roadside duel, this novel’s title character faces a traveling Basque man whose only shield is a pillow grabbed in a panic. After skipping out on an unpaid bill at an inn, this character’s squire gets tossed in a blanket by rowdy guests.
tossups.r: This character’s library of romance novels is burned by a priest, a barber, and his niece, who hope the loss will cure his madness. For 10 points, name this novel by Miguel de Cervantes about a gentleman who renames himself a knight-errant and fights windmills.

tossups.p: This novel was written to poke fun at the wildly popular romance novels about knights that were published across Spain. Its title character mistakes an ordinary barber’s metal washbasin for the magical Helmet of Mambrino, a treasure from those same kinds of romance stories.
tossups.r: Published in two parts, a 1605 Part One and a 1615 Part Two, the novel follows a gentleman who renames himself a wandering knight. For 10 points, name this novel whose title character rides Rocinante and fights windmills with his squire, Sancho Panza.

tossups.p: This novel’s title character is nicknamed the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance for his sad, hollow-cheeked face. He also drinks the Balsam of Fierabras, a fictional magic cure, and ends up violently sick rather than healed.
tossups.r: He idealizes a peasant girl whom he renames Dulcinea and treats as if she were a noble lady. For 10 points, name this novel in which a Spanish gentleman loses his mind reading tales of chivalry and sets off with his squire, Sancho Panza, to fight imaginary giants.

tossups.p: A prank-playing duke names this novel’s squire governor of the fictional island of Barataria, an island the title character had long promised him. Earlier, that same squire is tossed in a blanket by inn guests after his master skips out on paying the bill.
tossups.r: The squire’s donkey, Dapple, is also stolen and later recovered. For 10 points, name this novel by Miguel de Cervantes in which an aging gentleman renames himself a knight-errant and attacks windmills he mistakes for giants.

tossups.p: This novel claims to be translated from the notebooks of a fictional Arab historian named Cide Hamete Benengeli. Its title character destroys a traveling puppet show run by a man called Master Pedro, convinced the puppets’ enemies are real soldiers.
tossups.r: He also attacks cloth merchants from Toledo for refusing to call his imaginary lady-love the most beautiful woman alive. For 10 points, name this novel whose title knight rides Rocinante and fights windmills with his squire, Sancho Panza.

trap.title: Quixote or Sancho?
trap.body: Several famous clues are really about his squire, Sancho Panza, not about him directly: the donkey Dapple belongs to Sancho, and it is Sancho (not his master) who gets tossed in a blanket and later named governor of Barataria.
trap.fix: Check who is doing the action in the clue. If the clue says “his squire does X” or “his companion is made governor,” the answer is still the knight himself, not Sancho.
trap.line: Real answer line: Don Quixote [“kee-HOH-tay”] (accept Alonso Quixano).
